title: Blade Guards and Blade Soakers: How to Store Short Track Blades and Stop Rust
thumbnail_text: Your blades are rusting in your bag

scenes.heading: Blade Guards and Blade Soakers
scenes.sub: How to store short track blades and stop rust
scenes.chapter: Why blades rust in the bag
scenes.narration: In the next few minutes you will learn the difference between blade guards and blade soakers, and a ninety second routine that stops your short track blades from rusting. You will also learn how to read rust once it starts. For most skaters, the blades are the most expensive part of the setup. And the thing that kills them is rarely a crash or a bad sharpen. It is water. A thin film of melted ice, left on ground steel inside a closed bag, is enough to start pitting an edge. Once rust bites into the running surface, you have to grind metal away to get back to clean steel. Every sharpen after that takes life off the blade.

scenes.heading: Why short track steel rusts fast
bullets: Ice is water, and it stays on the blade
Blade steel is hardened for edges, not rust
Grit holds moisture against the steel
A sealed bag keeps the air saturated
scenes.narration: Here is why it happens so quickly. When you skate, the edge melts a very thin layer of ice. That is what lets you glide. When you step off, that water is still sitting on freshly ground steel. Blade steel is hardened to hold an edge, not to resist corrosion. So it reacts easily with moisture and oxygen. Two things speed this up. The first is grit. Dust, floor debris and stray fibres hold water against the steel long after it would have dried. The second is a sealed space. Zip damp skates inside a bag, and the moisture has nowhere to go. The air around the blade stays wet for hours.

scenes.heading: What sits on your steel
scenes.narration: This diagram shows a blade in cross section, just after a session. Along the top of the steel there is a thin film of water, shown in blue. Mixed in with it are small grey specks of grit and dust. Down at the bottom is the edge, and that is where the orange spots of rust begin. The edge is the thinnest part of the steel, so it is the first part to corrode. That is the worst place for rust to start, because the edge is the part that does all the work on the ice.

scenes.heading: Hard guards are for walking
bullets: Fit them the moment you step off
Take them off at the barrier
Wipe grit out of the channel
Check the spring still holds firm
Never store skates in guards
scenes.narration: Hard guards are the rigid plastic covers. They have one job, which is to protect your edges while you walk. Rink floors, rubber matting, tiles and concrete all chew steel. One unguarded step onto a hard floor can put a nick in an edge that you will feel all session. So put your guards on the moment you step off the ice, before you walk anywhere. Take them off at the barrier, not halfway across the room. Now and then, wipe out the inside of the guard, because grit collects in the channel. Check that the spring still holds firm, because a slack guard drops off mid walk. And never store your skates in guards.

scenes.heading: Soakers are for the bag
bullets: Terry cloth pulls water off the steel
Use them for storage and travel
Two sizes, chosen by blade length
Never walk in soakers
scenes.narration: Soakers are the soft fabric covers, and they do the opposite job. They are for storage, not walking. The terry cloth inside wicks water off the blade and holds it away from the steel. A hard guard seals moisture in against the metal. A soaker draws it out and lets it dry. The StayBent Blade Soakers come in two sizes, chosen by blade length. Small and medium fits blades from thirteen to sixteen inches. Medium and large fits sixteen and a half to eighteen inches. Measure your own blade before you order. And remember, soakers give no protection on a hard floor, so never walk in them.

scenes.heading: Two covers, two jobs
scenes.narration: Here are the two side by side. On the left, in green, are hard guards, for walking. The rigid shell takes the abuse of floors, matting and concrete. But if you store your skates in them, they trap water, so take them off at home. On the right, in blue, are soakers, for the bag. The terry cloth pulls moisture off the steel and holds it away. Use them for storage and transport, and dry them out between sessions. Most skaters carry both, and swap over at the barrier. One without the other leaves a gap.

scenes.heading: The ninety second routine
scenes.narration: This is the routine that protects your steel, in five steps. Do it every time, even after a short session, because twenty minutes on the ice leaves just as much water on the blade as two hours. Step one, guards on at the barrier. Do not take a single step on bare steel. Step two, sit down and take the boots off. Step three, pull the guards off and wipe the whole blade dry. Do the running surface, both sides, the cups and the mounting bolts. Water hides in the corners around the cups. Step four, let the steel air for a few minutes while you change. Step five, soakers on for the bag.

scenes.heading: Finish the job at home
bullets: Open the bag as soon as you get home
Pull the soakers off
Let blades and soakers dry fully
A damp soaker holds water on the steel
scenes.narration: The routine does not end at the rink. When you get home, take the skates out of the bag and pull the soakers off. Let both the blades and the soakers dry fully before your next session. This step matters more than it sounds. A soaker that stays damp all the time holds moisture against the steel instead of drawing it away. That turns your best blade care habit into your worst one. While you are drying the blade, you can also check the edge. Run a fingertip lightly along the side of the edge, never across it. If you feel a small raised lip, called a burr, a few light passes with a deburr stone will clean it up.

scenes.heading: How far has the rust gone
scenes.narration: Not all rust is the same problem. It runs through three stages, and this diagram shows each one. Stage one, in green, is a grey haze. Bright steel has gone dull and cloudy, but nothing has been eaten away. Wipe it dry and keep skating. Do not start grinding at it. Stage two, in orange, is speckling. Fine orange dots, often near the edge or the cups. Act now. Work along the blade with the fine side of a combination stone, using light, even pressure, then deburr. Stage three, in red, is pitting. These are craters in the running surface. Only a deep grind removes them, so take the blade to a technician and expect to lose some blade life.

scenes.heading: Humidity and travel
bullets: Cold steel sweats in warm, humid air
Wipe again once the blade warms up
Store skates in a cool, dry room
Travel in soakers, never in guards
scenes.narration: Skaters in India face an extra problem. You step out of a cold, dry rink into warm, humid air. Condensation forms on cold steel almost at once, just like a cold bottle sweating on a hot afternoon. The blade can be dry when you pack it and wet ten minutes later. So change when you dry, not how. Wipe the blades before you leave the building, fit soakers, then wipe again once everything has warmed up at home. In the monsoon, and at coastal rinks, treat that second wipe as compulsory. Store skates in an air conditioned room, not a cupboard or a balcony. When you travel, blades go in soakers, never in hard guards. Open the bag as soon as you arrive, and carry a spare pair of soakers on long trips.

scenes.heading: Mistakes and replacing covers
bullets: Replace guards that rattle or crack
Replace soakers gone thin or hard
No skates left in the car boot
Never dry with a damp towel
Wipe along the blade, not across
scenes.narration: Guards and soakers both wear out. A guard is finished when the spring no longer holds it firm, when the shell cracks, or when the blade sits loose and rattles. A soaker is finished when the cloth goes thin, matted or hard, or holds a smell that will not wash out. Hand wash soakers in cool water and air dry them fully. A few mistakes to avoid. Do not leave skates in the boot of a car, where heat and humidity keep cycling. Do not dry the blade with a damp cloth or a used towel. Do not forget the cups, lips and bolts. And always wipe along the blade, not across the edge, because that is how skaters cut their fingers.

scenes.heading: Guards for walking, soakers for the bag
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: If you remember one thing, make it this. Guards are for walking. Soakers are for storage. Swap them over at the barrier, wipe the steel dry every single time, and let everything dry fully at home. Ninety seconds of habit is what separates blades that last for years from blades that pit in a single season. The full guide, with the rust stages, the frequently asked questions and the soaker sizing, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
